prompt: My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself. I get into these depressed like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.
response_text:
I'm really sorry you've been through that kind of abandonment—it makes complete sense that it would leave you feeling wrecked and wary. What you're describing, that intense emotional response when people you care about aren't available, is a very common reaction to past relationship wounds. It doesn't mean something is fundamentally wrong with you; it means you've been hurt and your mind is trying to protect you from being hurt again.

The fact that you recognize these patterns and want to grow is actually a really meaningful first step. Healing from abandonment often benefits from working with a therapist or counselor who can help you understand these triggers, build self-compassion, and develop healthier ways to cope with those painful feelings when they come up. You don't have to figure this out alone, and you deserve support as you work through it.

prompt: I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?
response_text:
It's completely normal to feel nervous before starting therapy, and worrying about crying is one of the most common fears people have. The good news is that therapists are specifically trained to handle tears — crying is something they see regularly, and they view it as a natural, healthy part of the process, not something embarrassing. You won't be judged or seen as weak. In fact, tears often signal that something meaningful is being explored.

If you do cry, your therapist will likely offer you a moment, maybe some tissues, and gently help you through it at whatever pace feels right. You're also allowed to set boundaries — you can tell them you're nervous about crying, or ask for a break if you need one. Many people find that once they've had that first session, the anxiety eases considerably. You're taking a brave step by going, and you don't have to have it all together when you walk in.

prompt: I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?
response_text:
It's completely normal to feel nervous and shaky going into therapy, even after a few sessions. Therapy asks you to open up about deeply personal things, often with someone you're still getting to know. That vulnerability can trigger your body's stress response, which might explain the shakiness. Building trust and comfort with a therapist takes time, and a couple of sessions is still very early in that process.

If the nervousness feels overwhelming or gets in the way of you engaging in sessions, it's absolutely worth mentioning to your therapist. They're used to hearing this and can help you explore what's coming up and find ways to help you feel more at ease. You might also find that the intensity lessens as you build more rapport and familiarity. There's no timeline you need to follow — your experience is valid wherever you are in the process.

prompt: I have been with my boyfriend for more than a year. He recently got a new job and travels a lot. I’m not used to him being gone all the time. I feel as though he has forgotten about me because he does not talk with me as much and doesn’t keep me up to date on everything that he does throughout the day, which he used to. I feel lost, sad and unwanted. This is really a tough new challenge. I just want to break up with him, but I love him so much. I don’t know why he is acting this way lately. I believe I have separation anxiety. Is there anything that I can do to help me cope with this while he is out of town?
response_text:
It sounds like you're going through a really difficult transition, and it's completely understandable to feel sad and unsettled when a relationship dynamic changes so suddenly. What you're experiencing may well be related to separation anxiety, and those feelings of being unwanted are valid even if they don't reflect his actual feelings toward you.

Consider having an honest, gentle conversation with him when he's home about how you've been feeling, focusing on expressing your needs rather than accusing him of neglect. In the meantime, coping strategies can include staying connected through scheduled check-ins that work for both of you, filling your time with activities and people that bring you fulfillment, journaling your feelings, and perhaps speaking with a counselor who can help you develop tools to manage the anxiety. Remember that his behavior likely reflects the demands of a new job rather than a change in how he feels about you, but you still deserve to feel valued and connected in your relationship.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're dealing with all of this — racing thoughts, poor sleep, and anxiety after a head injury is an exhausting combination, and it's especially frustrating when medication options haven't worked for you. Since you've had strong physical reactions to medications, it's important to talk with your doctor about those specific side effects so they can explore alternatives or non-medication approaches that may be gentler on your system.

In the meantime, some people find relief with grounding techniques like slow box breathing — inhale for four counts, hold four, exhale four, hold four — which can help calm your nervous system without any side effects. Progressive muscle relaxation, where you tense and release muscle groups one at a time, may also help with both anxiety and sleep. Reducing screen time before bed, keeping your room cool and dark, and trying a guided sleep meditation can make a difference too. You might also ask your doctor about whether a referral to a neuropsychologist or a therapist experienced with brain injury could be helpful — there are therapy approaches that don't involve medication at all. You're not alone in this, and it's okay to keep searching for what works for you.

prompt: I think I'm annoying and bothersome, but my girlfriend says I'm just fine. I don't think so, I think I'm stressing everyone else out
response_text:
It sounds really painful to carry that belief about yourself, especially when it conflicts with what someone close to you is saying. Sometimes our inner critic can be much harsher than reality, and it can be hard to accept reassurance even when it's genuine.

Your girlfriend's perspective matters — she knows you and is telling you that you're not a burden. It's okay to not fully believe that right away, but try to stay open to the possibility that she might be seeing something you can't. If these feelings are persistent and affecting your relationships or wellbeing, talking to a mental health professional could help you understand where this self-critical voice comes from and how to quiet it. You deserve to feel okay being yourself.

prompt: When my daughter is stressed about a silly thing from school, she starts crying and freaking out. She is a bright student, always has a 4.0, but I am afraid she is stressing too much. I’m afraid it’s going to break her. I don't know if I should get her to a doctor or someone because this is not normal.
response_text:
It sounds like you're deeply attuned to your daughter's wellbeing, and your concern makes sense. Intense emotional reactions to stress, especially in a high-achieving student, can be a sign that she's carrying more than she can manage on her own. That doesn't necessarily mean something is "wrong" with her, but it does mean she may need more support than she's currently getting.

Reaching out to her pediatrician or a licensed mental health professional is a reasonable and caring step. They can help assess what's going on and offer tools to manage stress before it escalates. In the meantime, you can also gently let her know that her worth isn't tied to her grades and that you're there for her no matter what. Sometimes just feeling truly heard and supported at home can ease some of that pressure.

prompt: My ex-wife married and used me to have a child. She now uses that child as a pawn. I know my child misses me, but I need to move on and not live in the past. How do I do this? Do I see my child as much as possible or very little? Is it more confusing for the child?
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pain from this situation, and it's understandable to feel torn. Children generally benefit from having consistent, loving relationships with both parents when it's safe to do so. Rather than seeing your child very little, maintaining regular, predictable contact can provide stability and reassurance—children are often more resilient than we give them credit for, and what matters most is that they feel loved and secure with you. The confusion tends to come more from inconsistency or conflict between parents than from simply having two involved parents.

That said, every situation is unique, and a family therapist or counselor could help you think through what arrangement would best support your child's emotional needs while also helping you process your own feelings about the past. If there are custody or visitation concerns, a family law professional can help clarify your rights and options. You don't have to figure this out alone, and reaching out for support is a sign of strength, not weakness.

prompt: I just feel sad all the time and I don't like anyone in my family. I feel like they're trying to control me and won't let me grow.
response_text:
I'm sorry you're feeling this way. It sounds really painful to feel sad all the time and to feel like the people closest to you are holding you back instead of supporting you. Your feelings are valid, and it's okay to want space and independence.

Feeling controlled by family can be especially confusing because these are people who are supposed to care about you. Sometimes talking to a counselor or therapist can help you sort through these feelings and figure out healthy ways to set boundaries or communicate what you need. If you're in the U.S., you can text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor, or call 988 if things ever feel overwhelming. You don't have to figure this out alone.

You deserve to grow and to feel like your own person. Please consider reaching out to someone you trust or a mental health professional who can support you through this.

prompt: Can a counselor take sides with one parent and allow a parent to order the child to tell the counselor "every detail" about what happened during the other parent’s visitation in order to help build a case for child custody?
response_text:
That practice would generally be considered unethical. Counselors are expected to remain neutral, especially in custody-related situations, and to prioritize the child's well-being rather than serving as a tool to build one parent's case. A counselor should not allow a parent to direct the child to report detailed information about the other parent's visitation for litigation purposes, as this can place the child in a stressful loyalty conflict and cause emotional harm.

If you have concerns about a counselor's conduct, you can consider filing a complaint with their licensing board or speaking with a family law attorney about your options. You might also request a court-appointed evaluator or an independent child therapist if a neutral professional is needed. It's important that any professional involved focuses on the child's best interests rather than advocacy for one parent. If you're navigating a difficult custody situation, reaching out to a trusted family law attorney or a local family services organization can help you understand your rights and next steps.

prompt: I have four children. One of them is in her 20s, and she cannot afford to go, nor can I pay for her. She went last year for two weeks by herself.
response_text:
It sounds like you care deeply about your daughter and want her to get the help she needs, but the financial barrier is real and stressful. That's a difficult position for both of you.

There may be lower-cost options worth exploring. Many community mental health centers offer sliding-scale fees based on income, and some therapists offer reduced rates. If she's in the U.S., she can call 211 to learn about local resources, or check NAMI (nami.org) for free support groups and guidance. If she had a positive experience last year, the facility she went to may also have payment plans or scholarships she could ask about. Online therapy platforms can sometimes be more affordable too.

It's also okay to acknowledge that you can't fix this financially — that doesn't mean you're failing her. Encouraging her to take small steps, like connecting with a support group or a primary care doctor who can point her toward resources, can still make a meaningful difference.

prompt: I am divorced and happily remarried. Our blended family of children are in their 20s. My youngest, age 20, continues to call me crazy and favors her dad. He was abusive to me, and I left with injuries. He never wanted kids, and I did. He paid child support only through forced wage earners. Now my daughters favor him after all the sacrifices I made for them the past 15 years as a single mom. I don’t deny them a relationship with their dad, but to be called crazy and then watch them hang out with him hurts me to the very core. I’m not sure how to handle this.
response_text:
It sounds incredibly painful to be called "crazy" and to watch your daughters favor their father after everything you went through and sacrificed. Your hurt is completely understandable—anyone would feel deeply wounded in your shoes.

It's worth remembering that adult children often have limited or incomplete understanding of their parents' experiences, and they may be processing family dynamics in their own way, on their own timeline. That doesn't make their behavior acceptable, especially the name-calling, which you have every right to address by setting a clear boundary: you can let them know you won't engage in conversations where you're spoken to disrespectfully.

You might also consider speaking with a therapist who can help you navigate the grief, anger, and complex emotions this situation brings. A professional can offer personalized guidance on communication strategies and boundaries with your adult children. In the meantime, leaning on your spouse and other trusted supports can help you feel less alone as you work through this.

prompt: I'm always told I'm not good enough or trying hard enough. I put 100% in to every thing. I'm worn out, I've worked on all of my family relationships, I'm doing great in school, I'm kind to those in need and otherwise. I stick to my religious beliefs and leave room for mistakes and learn from others so I don't have to make as many and the ones I do I learn from. Somehow it's still not good enough and nothing I do works. Nothing has changed, and I feel hopeless. Any suggestions or ideas?
response_text:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to give so much of yourself and still feel like it's never enough. What you're describing — the kindness, the effort, the willingness to learn — those are genuinely admirable qualities, and I hope you can recognize that the problem may not be with you, but with impossible expectations that no one could meet.

Sometimes the voices telling us we're "not enough" come from others, and sometimes they become an internal voice we've absorbed. It might help to ask: whose standard are you being measured against, and is that standard actually fair? You might also consider speaking with a counselor or therapist who can help you explore these feelings of hopelessness in a supportive space. If these feelings become overwhelming or you start having thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or someone you trust right away.

You deserve care too — including from yourself.

prompt: It's been almost a year since my ex-boyfriend broke up with me after he cheated on me many times. I had found out about a month before, but I hadn't told him I knew because I didn't want us to break up. I used to have very low self-esteem, and I think it might have to do with my dad being an alcoholic. My father cheated on my mother when I was little. I wonder if this pain has to do with that. My ex-boyfriend and I were only dating for five months, but I still can't get over this betrayal. I'm not sure what to feel to get over it: forgiveness? Hate? He helped me financially after our break up by lending me $3000, so I'm grateful for that. I still hate him for what he did and still want him to like me although we're not even talking anymore. We follow each other on Instagram and that's it. I feel like I still need his validation. This is haunting me day and night. I want to focus on my new relationship and goals, but I keep obsessing over this and keep checking my ex-boyfriend's Instagram and Facebook. I feel so bad and keep having nightmares.
response_text:
It makes complete sense that this betrayal is affecting you so deeply, especially given what you witnessed with your father. Childhood experiences shape how we understand trust, love, and self-worth, and it's very common for old wounds to resurface when we experience similar pain as adults. The conflicting feelings you have—gratitude, hate, wanting his validation—are all valid and normal responses to betrayal. You don't need to force forgiveness or any particular emotion; healing isn't about choosing the "right" feeling.

The social media checking is likely reinforcing the obsession and keeping the wound open. Consider muting or unfollowing him to give yourself space to focus on your present life. Since this is affecting your sleep, causing nightmares, and interfering with your current relationship, talking to a therapist could help you process both the recent betrayal and the earlier experiences with your father. You deserve to heal and feel whole without needing validation from someone who hurt you. Be gentle with yourself—you're carrying a lot, and it's okay to seek support.

prompt: I'm a male in my 20s. My girlfriend is in her late 30s. She's great. She's funny and smart, she has a big heart, and we have an excellent sex life. She recently moved in with me partially because she wanted to and partially because she had no place to go. We fight a lot. It’s mostly my fault, I must admit. She doesn't like my insecurity and lack of trust I have for her. I have trust issues. Also, I can't fathom why a woman like her is with me, so I'm always dreading when a better dude will come along. I don't think she's happy. She's very submissive and she loves me very much, but also the fact that she has nowhere to go must be influencing her decision to stay. I love her so much, but my jealousy is not likely to diminish. I never believed in the whole "If you love them, let them go," but I do now. I really want her to be happy. Should I end it with her? She has no place to go so I feel like I can’t break up with her. I’m literally trapped.
response_text:
It takes real courage to recognize how your insecurity and trust issues are affecting someone you love. The fact that you want her happiness—even if it means stepping back—shows genuine care, not weakness. Feeling trapped by her housing situation is a heavy burden, but staying in a relationship out of guilt or logistics isn't sustainable for either of you, and it may actually deepen the resentment and jealousy you're already struggling with.

Consider talking with a therapist individually to work through the trust issues and self-worth concerns you've described. You might also try having an honest, compassionate conversation with her about how you're feeling—not to make a final decision in one talk, but to open the door to understanding what she actually wants. She may have more clarity than you're giving her credit for. Ultimately, both of you deserve a relationship built on trust and mutual choice, not obligation. Whatever you decide, getting professional support can help you navigate this with more confidence and less guilt.

prompt: About 3 years ago or so I was skinny, but I was still ugly. I really do want to change that but I've tried 3 times. Now can I try but don't stop. At school I get bullied about my weight and my ugliness and I have been bullied my whole life that I believe them. How can I stop thinking about them and don't let it get in my head? My parents said I don't weight that much but, they do think I am fat but, they tell me I am not. I told my parents that I need to go to a therapist, but they think I am fine and I think they don't want to deal with it.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're going through this. Being bullied about your appearance is incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense that years of those messages have affected how you see yourself. What the bullies say reflects their cruelty, not your worth or reality.

It's really tough when your parents aren't taking your need for support seriously. You deserve to talk to someone who can help. Consider speaking with a school counselor—they can offer support during the school day and may be able to help your parents understand why therapy would be valuable. You can also reach out to free text or phone lines like Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741) or The Trevor Project if you need someone to talk to right away.

Your feelings are valid, and wanting help is a sign of strength, not weakness. Please keep advocating for yourself—you deserve support and kindness, including from yourself.

prompt: Everyone around me is much smarter and flaunts it. Everyone around me is skinny, and here I am trying to throw up so I'm not fat. Everything I do is wrong, and I can't seem to do anything right! No one else at school seems to feel the way I do! Is this normal teenage girls feelings? I don't think these feelings are normal.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this much pain. What you're describing — feeling like everyone else is smarter, thinner, better — and the urge to throw up to control your body, those feelings are heavy and exhausting. While many teens struggle with comparison and self-doubt, throwing up to try to change your body is harmful and is something worth talking about with a trusted adult or health professional who can support you.

You don't have to figure this out alone. Please consider reaching out to someone you trust — a parent, school counselor, doctor, or a helpline. In the US, you can text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor, or call the National Eating Disorders Association helpline at 1-800-931-2237. You deserve real support and care, not to suffer in silence. What you're feeling matters, and help is available.

prompt: I'm obsessing about a terrible breakup. Everything is a constant reminder. How do I move on?
response_text:
I'm sorry you're going through this—breakups can be genuinely painful, and it makes sense that reminders are everywhere right now. Your brain is processing a loss, and that takes time.

A few things that may help: First, try to limit your exposure to triggers when possible—muting or unfollowing your ex on social media, putting away photos or gifts for now. Second, when reminders do hit, try acknowledging the feeling without fighting it: "I'm missing them right now, and that's okay." Resisting the pain often makes it louder. Third, gently fill your schedule with small things that engage you—walking, calling a friend, trying a new routine. Not as a distraction from grief, but alongside it.

Consider journaling to get the looping thoughts out of your head and onto paper. If you find the obsessing is interfering with sleep, work, or daily life for more than a few weeks, talking to a counselor could be really valuable. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: I know that I need to get past my feelings for this person I fell in love with, but t's so difficult to move on because he showed me feelings I've never felt before. I feel like I don't want to be without my genuine love for him, but logically, I know I need to be without him. I can't discuss this with anybody in my life because the conditions surrounding our love are considered "wrong" by a lot of people. How can I get myself to just move on?
response_text:
It's incredibly hard to move on when someone opened emotional doors you didn't know existed. That grief is real, and it makes sense that you don't want to lose those feelings—they're part of you now, even if the relationship can't continue. You don't have to force yourself to stop loving someone overnight; healing often means learning to carry those feelings differently rather than erasing them.

The isolation of not being able to talk about this with people in your life must add another heavy layer. If possible, consider speaking with a counselor or therapist—confidentiality means you can be honest without judgment, and a professional can help you process both the love and the loss. You might also try journaling as a private outlet for now. Be gentle with yourself—moving on isn't a switch to flip, and you're allowed to grieve something that mattered deeply while still taking steps forward.

prompt: My wife just last week said she wants a divorce and it's all sudden. I understand that marriages have their ups and downs but I don't understand why she can't tell me why she wants a divorce. Should I fight for my family (daughter and wife)?
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're going through this. Having your wife ask for a divorce with no clear explanation is deeply painful and disorienting, especially when you're also thinking about your daughter and the family you've built together.

It's natural to want to fight for your family, and showing your commitment isn't wrong. However, "fighting for" a relationship works best when it means staying open, calm, and willing to listen rather than pressuring her for answers she may not be ready to give. Sometimes people struggle to articulate their feelings, or they need space before they can. You might let her know you love her and your family, that you're willing to work on things together, and that you'll respect whatever pace she needs. Couples counseling could also help create a safe space for honest conversation, even if she's unsure.

In the meantime, please lean on trusted friends, family, or a counselor for your own support. This is a heavy burden to carry alone, and you deserve care too.

prompt: I keep on begging him to come back. I am so unhappy with him but am so scared of being a single parent to our son. I was abused as a little girl and that has made to be very abusive to men. What should I do...
response_text:
It takes real courage to share this, and the fact that you're reflecting on these patterns shows how much you care about yourself and your son. It's completely understandable to feel scared about the future, especially when past wounds are so deeply tied to how you relate to others now.

Healing from childhood abuse and breaking cycles of harmful behavior often requires support that goes beyond what anyone can do alone. A therapist or counselor can help you process those early experiences, understand how they shape your relationships now, and develop healthier ways of coping. You deserve that support, and your son deserves a mom who is healing and whole. Consider reaching out to a domestic violence or trauma-informed counseling service in your area, as they understand these complexities with compassion and without judgment. You're not alone in this, and asking "what should I do" is already an important first step.

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response_text:
Reducing the risk of divorce often comes down to consistent, intentional effort in the relationship. Couples who stay connected tend to prioritize open communication, making time to really listen to each other without judgment. They also work on managing conflict constructively—addressing issues directly rather than letting resentment build, and being willing to repair after disagreements rather than staying withdrawn.

It's also important to nurture friendship and appreciation within the partnership. Small gestures of kindness, expressing gratitude, and making space for shared activities can strengthen the emotional bond over time. Being realistic about challenges and willing to seek support—whether through couples counseling or trusted resources—can also make a meaningful difference. Every relationship faces difficulties, and reaching out for help early rather than waiting until things feel overwhelming is a sign of strength, not failure.

prompt: I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you experienced this. Crying is a completely normal human response to stress, and feeling emotional at a new job—especially your first one—doesn't make you weak or unprofessional. What you went through sounds really overwhelming, and it's understandable that you're worried about how things stand now.

That said, no one should be pushed to tears at work, especially a teenager just starting out. If your boss's management style is making you feel this way, it might be worth talking to a trusted adult—a parent, guardian, teacher, or school counselor—who can help you think through your options. You deserve a workplace that treats you with respect, and if this environment isn't healthy for you, it's okay to consider whether it's the right fit. Your wellbeing matters far more than any job.

prompt: My wife is always accusing me of cheating and telling me that I'm doing things she finds disrespectful even when I don't mean it like that. For example, she gets offended when I call someone at work "sweetheart." I wish I had a penny for every time she accused me of cheating on her. She doesn't, and never will say she was wrong. How do I get her to understand?
response_text:
That sounds exhausting and painful to navigate. It's hard to feel constantly under suspicion, especially when you don't intend harm.

One approach is to shift the conversation from defending yourself to understanding her feelings. Try saying something like, "I can see this really hurts you, and I want to understand what's behind it." This doesn't mean accepting false accusations, but it may open a more productive dialogue. Her reactions may stem from insecurity, past experiences, or anxiety rather than anything you're actually doing.

That said, you can't force her to see your perspective if she's not ready. Couples counseling could provide a neutral space where both of you feel heard and where patterns like this can be explored safely. A therapist can help facilitate conversations that feel impossible to have on your own.

In the meantime, it's also fair to set gentle boundaries, like expressing that constant accusations are affecting your wellbeing and the relationship. You deserve to feel trusted and respected too.

prompt: I am in a high stress position for a tech company. I am being overworked and underpaid for my contributions and it is not only giving me anxiety, but also demoralizing. What can I do to manage my stress?
response_text:
That sounds incredibly draining, and it's completely valid to feel both anxious and demoralized when your effort isn't being recognized or compensated fairly. Your well-being matters more than any job.

In the short term, try to set firmer boundaries around your work hours—log off when the day is done, take your breaks, and resist the pressure to be constantly available. Outside of work, even small rituals like a short walk, deep breathing, or talking with a trusted friend can help release tension. It may also be worth having an honest conversation with your manager about workload and compensation, or exploring whether an internal transfer or job search could lead to a healthier environment. You deserve a role that respects your contributions and your humanity.

If the anxiety starts to feel unmanageable or spills into other areas of your life, consider reaching out to a mental health professional or an employee assistance program if your company offers one. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: I've worked with this guy for about three years now, and I knew the first time I saw him that I was attracted. Over time, he became a very dear friend, and we talked about our relationship problems, family, dreams, and so on. There was always flirtation with us, and one day pretty recently, it progressed to making out. We agreed to keep it quiet, and we did, but in the back of my mind, I hoped it would become something more. It didn't, and three months later, I'm still not over it. I'm trying so hard to maintain the friendship because that's what he wants. We're no longer in the same office, which I thought would help me get over these feelings, but we still talk about work, and he's constantly touching me, so I'm still very drawn to him. He's a hugger and such a sweet guy, so I find myself fantasizing all the time about what could have been and what could still be, but he's clearly not interested. He's younger than me and prefers model types, but I see him checking me out a lot, which gives me hope. How do I get him out of my system and still maintain the friendship?
response_text:
It sounds like you're in a really painful spot—holding onto hope while also knowing he hasn't shown genuine interest in more. That mixed signaling, especially the physical closeness, makes it much harder to move on because it keeps feeding those fantasies.

Honestly, maintaining the friendship as it currently exists may not be realistic right now. His casual touching and attention are giving you false hope, even if he doesn't intend it that way. To get him out of your system, you likely need real distance—not just a different office, but boundaries on conversation frequency and physical contact. You can be kind but honest: something like, "I value our friendship, but I need some space to reset." A true friend will respect that. Also, be gentle with yourself—three years of connection and attraction don't disappear quickly. Consider redirecting that emotional energy toward people and activities that nourish you outside of this dynamic. If the friendship is meant to survive, it can withstand a period of distance while you heal.

prompt: Does this go against any ethical codes? Are there legal ramifications?
response_text:
I appreciate you reaching out, but I don't have enough context to understand what specific situation or action you're referring to. Without knowing more details, I can't speak to whether something might conflict with ethical codes or have legal implications.

If your concern involves something that happened to you or someone else—such as a boundary violation, mistreatment, or something that felt wrong—I'd encourage you to consider speaking with a trusted professional, an advocate, or a legal advisor who can give you guidance tailored to your situation. You deserve clarity and support in navigating whatever you're facing.

prompt: I am a survivor of multiple sexual abuse/rape experiences. Triggers are having an effect on my daily life and my sexual relationship with my partner. I'm trying to learn to cope with them.

prompt: That phrase makes me crazy. prompt: My husband took a job out of state for the next year and seems to be a different person. prompt: My husband and I have been together since high school. We have been married going on for nearly ten years, and we have three beautiful children. prompt: I have been with my husband for almost 7 years. We got engaged a little after 5 years of being together. prompt: Can a therapist have a client admitted to an eating disorder treatment center if the client does not want to go?
response_text:
In most cases, a therapist cannot force a client into eating disorder treatment without their consent unless the client is in immediate, life-threatening danger. If someone's eating disorder has caused severe medical instability—such as dangerously low weight, electrolyte imbalances, or risk of organ failure—a therapist or medical professional may initiate an emergency hold or hospitalization to protect their life. This process varies depending on local laws and the specific circumstances.

If you're navigating this situation, it's important to know that treatment is generally most effective when someone is willing to participate. If you're concerned about yourself or someone else, reaching out to a healthcare provider, a crisis line, or an eating disorder helpline can help clarify options and provide guidance. You deserve support and care, and there are people who can help you explore what feels right.

prompt: I've been bulimic for about 6 years now. I'm in my early 20s. I am about to start back to school to become an RN, and I really need to get better once and for all. prompt: I have a problem with binge eating, especially during times of stress. response_text:
Thank you for sharing something so personal and painful. What you're describing—binge eating followed by compensatory exercise—is a recognized pattern, and it makes sense that stress and shame fuel the cycle. You're not alone in this, and it's not a failure of willpower.

Some strategies that can help: practice urge surfing—when you feel the urge to binge, try to pause and sit with the feeling for even five minutes, noticing it without acting. Identify your stress triggers and experiment with alternative coping responses like reaching out to someone, journaling, or grounding exercises. After a binge, try to resist the urge to "fix" it through exercise—instead, speak to yourself with the compassion you'd offer a friend. Working with a therapist who specializes in eating concerns can be incredibly valuable for addressing the deeper patterns, and I'd really encourage you to consider that step.

Breaking a cycle that's been present since your teens takes time and patience. Please be gentle with yourself as you work through this.

prompt: I hardly eat. But I gain weight instead of lose weight. Why?
response_text:
It can be really frustrating and confusing to feel like you're eating very little yet still gaining weight. It's also possible that what feels like "hardly eating" may still include enough calories to maintain or gain weight, depending on the foods involved.

Because weight changes can be tied to complex medical factors, it's a good idea to talk with a healthcare provider who can help you understand what's happening in your body. They can check for underlying conditions and help you find a balanced approach to eating that supports your health. You deserve to feel well and have answers, so please consider reaching out to a professional who can support you.

prompt: I have no self control over food. Most people stop when they've had enough, but I keep eating for the pleasure of it. Especially with sweets - I'm never done eating dessert.
response_text:
It sounds really frustrating to feel like food has that kind of pull over you, and it's brave to name it so honestly. What you're describing isn't simply a willpower problem—eating for pleasure activates reward pathways in the brain, and sugary foods are particularly good at hijacking those signals. Many people experience this, so you're not broken or weak.

A few things that can help: avoiding keeping sweets in the house so the impulse is harder to act on, eating satisfying protein- and fiber-rich meals earlier in the day to reduce cravings, and practicing pausing for a few minutes when the urge hits—sometimes the intensity fades. Consider speaking with a therapist or registered dietitian who understands emotional and reward-based eating; they can help you build a healthier relationship with food without shame or restriction extremes. You deserve support with this, not judgment.

prompt: We've been in a long distance relationship for two and a half years. I recently saw his phone and saw the people he texts the most and one of them was a female coworker. I don't know how to approach this situation. How do I ask him about it?.

prompt: I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it. How should I deal with this?

prompt: I'm in a relationship with my fiancé and I currently found out that she's been cheating on me with a co-worker. I was very upset none the less. prompt: We’ve been together almost three years. We argue and he ends it by telling me he doesn’t love me. prompt: He said he would try and he never did. It's been nine months, and this is making me worse. Today, he said I have to respect whatever decision he makes. Is that true? prompt: How can I control my anxiety when I have Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
response_text:
Managing anxiety with OCD can feel overwhelming, but there are strategies that may help. It gradually helps you face fears without engaging in compulsions, reducing anxiety over time. Mindfulness practices, grounding techniques, and learning to label intrusive thoughts as just thoughts can also be useful tools.

It's important to remember that anxiety often spikes before it gets better, and progress isn't always linear. Be patient with yourself. If you're not already connected with a therapist or counselor, reaching out to one can make a meaningful difference. You can also contact the International OCD Foundation or a crisis line like 988 (in the U.S.) if you need immediate support. You don't have to navigate this alone.

prompt: I am extremely possessive in my relationships and this is hurting my friendships. How can I fix my underlying issues?

It takes real self-awareness and courage to recognize this pattern and want to change it. A good starting point is to notice the thoughts and physical sensations that arise when you feel possessive urges. Are you afraid someone will leave? Do you feel you're not enough? Therapy can be incredibly helpful for unpacking these root causes and building healthier relationship patterns. In the moment, practicing pausing before reacting, challenging anxious thoughts, and allowing your friends space without trying to control their choices can help you respond differently over time. Change is absolutely possible with patience and practice.

prompt: I start to think of an issue that doesn't even matter or something bad that happened years ago. Then, I cry, pull at my hair, plug my ears, hit myself, and throw things. prompt: I am lazy. I am very aware of the problem and try to talk myself out of it all the time, but I never seem to shake the habits. Consider trying a few small shifts: break tasks into tiny, almost ridiculously small steps (just open the document, just write one sentence), and try working for only five minutes to lower the barrier to starting. Sometimes removing the pressure to "do it well" and just focusing on "doing something" helps break the cycle. It might also be worth talking to a school counselor or academic support service—they see this pattern frequently and can help you figure out what's really getting in your way. prompt: I never get infections or scars or anything, and it doesn't bother me if it gets filled up with blood or something, but I'm concerned.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response_text:
That's a really good question to ask, and it's understandable to want clarity about your privacy. Generally, a past therapist cannot disclose your information to a current therapist without your written consent. Mental health professionals are bound by confidentiality laws like HIPAA, which protect your records and communications.

There are some exceptions, such as imminent risk of harm, but routine sharing between providers requires your permission. If you'd like your therapists to coordinate care, you can sign a release of information authorizing that communication. You have the right to decide what gets shared and with whom.

If you're concerned about your privacy, it's completely okay to ask either therapist directly about their confidentiality policies. They should be able to explain clearly how your information is protected and what control you have over it.

prompt: I terminated my counseling relationship with a social worker several years ago. I am now realizing that I would like to begin counseling again. prompt: My boyfriend is in the hospital. They won’t tell me what’s wrong and if or when he’s coming back
response_text:
It's completely understandable to feel scared and frustrated when someone you care about is in the hospital and you're left without answers. prompt: What do you do when a therapist and a parent drugs a child and makes up lies in order to stop the other parent's custody visitation?

prompt: I have major depression, severe, PTSD, anxiety disorder, and personality disorder. I had an appointment with my doctor. I was very upset, and I shared with him about that particular drug.

prompt: How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Ethical guidelines also require counselors to terminate or refer when they recognize they're not the right fit for a client's needs, when boundaries become complicated, or when the therapeutic relationship isn't productive. Importantly, good termination isn't abrupt—it's planned, includes reviewing progress, discussing relapse-prevention strategies, and ensuring the client knows they can return if needed. If you're currently in counseling and wondering about this, it's completely okay to ask your counselor directly about their thoughts on your progress and timeline.

Informational interviews are very common, and most people are flattered to be asked. When you do connect, asking about their courses, how long they studied, and what they enjoy about their job are all wonderful questions. Good luck with your search!

prompt: I am an international student, and it is my first semester in graduate school in the United States. I faced a cultural shock, and I was so depressed when I arrived here. My counselor in the university was my savior. He helped me a great deal. Now I am going back to my country for a vacation. I was thinking to get him something special with my country's name on it, and I remembered that he likes wine. My country is known for that. Is it appropriate to give him wine as a gift after Christmas?
response_text:
It's really touching that you want to show your appreciation, and it's wonderful that your counselor helped you through such a difficult transition. That said, many university counseling centers have strict policies about gifts, and alcohol in particular can be problematic due to professional ethics and campus policies. Even with the best intentions, giving wine might put your counselor in an awkward position where they'd have to decline.

A heartfelt handwritten note expressing what their support meant to you is often the most cherished gift a counselor can receive. If you'd like to give something more, small, inexpensive items like a postcard or traditional candy from your country are usually more acceptable. You could also simply tell them in person how much their help meant to you. Many counselors say that knowing they made a difference is the greatest reward.

prompt: I'm worried I should see a therapist due to past events and current mental status. I'm just so unsure of how to ask my doctor about seeing someone.
response_text: It's completely understandable to feel unsure about bringing this up, and it's a positive step that you're considering support. When you see your doctor, you can keep it simple and direct. You might say something like, "I've been struggling with some things from my past and how I'm feeling now, and I think talking to someone could help. Can you refer me to a therapist?" Remember, doctors hear this often and are there to help you access the right care. You don't need to share everything all at once if you're not comfortable. You deserve support, and reaching out is a brave and important step toward healing.

prompt: These "jokes" are made about everything. They seem to have the need to say something "funny" about everything. It's not funny, just awkward.
response_text:
That sounds really exhausting. When someone feels compelled to make a joke about everything, it can feel dismissive, especially if you're trying to have a genuine conversation or share something meaningful. It's okay to find that awkward and frustrating.

You're allowed to set boundaries around this. A simple "I'd rather talk seriously about this" or "That joke doesn't land for me" can gently signal what you need. Some people use humor as a defense mechanism or a way to manage discomfort, but that doesn't mean you have to absorb it without comment. Your feelings about this are valid.

prompt: It's really hard to not have negative feelings about friends who don't put any effort into nourishing our relationship.
response_text:
It's completely valid to feel hurt and frustrated when friendships feel one-sided. You're investing care and energy, and it's painful when that isn't reciprocated. Those feelings don't make you a bad friend — they show you value connection deeply.

It might help to remember that people's capacity often shifts due to their own life circumstances, stress, or mental health, and their lack of effort may not be about you personally. That said, it's also okay to reassess where you place your energy. You deserve relationships that feel mutual and fulfilling. Consider gently expressing how you feel to friends you value — sometimes people genuinely don't realize. And if certain connections remain draining despite your efforts, it's okay to step back and make space for people who can meet you halfway.

prompt: I was “mentored” by this guy for a few years spiritually. It was okay at times, but other times, it was just weird. I try not to think about it too much, but a lot of manipulation and lying happened, yet no one else really believed me when I told them. It's like he's two different people, and no one else really sees that side of him. I was blamed for a lot of our troubles, and now we don't really talk much. I'm worried because he's in a trusted position of leadership and no one suspects anything. They just think I'm attacking his character. How do I know for sure?
response_text:
It's really painful when you've experienced manipulation and then others dismiss or doubt your account. What you're describing—someone presenting differently to others than they did to you, being blamed for problems, and feeling confused about what was real—are common experiences in manipulative relationships. The fact that others don't see it doesn't mean it didn't happen; many people who cause harm are skilled at maintaining a positive public image.

You don't need absolute certainty or external validation to trust your own experience. You lived it. You felt the impact. Writing down specific memories—what happened, how you felt—can help you reconnect with your own perspective rather than relying on others' interpretations. Consider talking with a counselor who understands spiritual or relational manipulation; they can help you process this without pressure to "prove" anything. Your concern about others potentially being affected is valid, but your primary responsibility is your own healing and wellbeing right now.

prompt: I would like to be able to have more positive relationships in the present.
response_text:
It's wonderful that you're focusing on building more positive relationships — that desire itself shows real self-awareness and hope. Meaningful connections often start with small steps: being curious about others, practicing active listening, and allowing yourself to be a little vulnerable when it feels safe to do so. Sometimes it also helps to reflect on what qualities you value most in relationships, so you can seek those out intentionally.

It's also okay to go at your own pace. Building trust and connection takes time, and every small interaction — a kind word, a moment of genuine presence — can be a step toward the relationships you want. If you find old patterns or fears getting in the way, consider talking with a counselor or therapist who can help you explore those barriers in a supportive space. You deserve fulfilling connections, and the fact that you're reaching for them matters.

prompt: They're calling me names like hypocrite and a baby even when they act in the same manner as I do. I'm tired of being called names. What should I do?
response_text:
It sounds really exhausting and hurtful to be called names, especially when it feels unfair and one-sided. You deserve to be treated with respect, and it's completely valid to feel tired of this.

One thing you might try is setting a clear boundary by calmly telling them how their words affect you and that you want the name-calling to stop. If they continue, it's okay to limit your interactions with them or walk away when it happens. Surrounding yourself with people who treat you kindly can also make a big difference. If this is happening at school or work, consider talking to a trusted adult, counselor, or supervisor who can help address the situation. You don't have to handle this alone, and your feelings matter.

prompt: How do you know you have the right therapist for you? How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?
response_text:
Finding the right therapist often comes down to how you feel in the room with them. A good fit usually means you feel heard, respected, and safe enough to be honest—even when it's hard. You don't have to feel instant comfort, but over time you should sense progress, collaboration, and trust.

You don't need to "train" your therapist, but you *can* guide the process. It's okay to share what helps and what doesn't—whether that's wanting more structure, needing gentle challenges, or preferring to lead the conversation. A skilled therapist will welcome that feedback and adjust. If you're unsure how to start, try saying something like, "I want to talk about what I need from our sessions." If you express your needs and feel dismissed or misunderstood over time, it's valid to seek someone else. Therapy works best when it's a partnership.

prompt: Does counseling really do anything that can help people?
response_text:
Yes, counseling can genuinely help many people. It provides a structured, nonjudgmental space to explore thoughts and emotions, understand patterns in behavior or relationships, and develop practical coping strategies. Research across decades shows that therapy can reduce symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress while improving overall well-being and quality of life.

That said, counseling isn't one-size-fits-all. The therapeutic approach, the connection between client and counselor, and a person's readiness to engage all matter. Some people notice changes quickly, while for others it's a gradual process. It's also okay if a particular therapist or style isn't the right fit—finding the right match can make a significant difference. If you're curious, reaching out for an initial session or consultation can be a low-pressure way to explore whether it feels helpful for you.

prompt: How does a person start the counseling process?
response_text:
Starting counseling can feel intimidating, but it's a positive step toward caring for your mental health. A good first move is to identify what you'd like support with — whether that's stress, anxiety, relationships, grief, or simply wanting to understand yourself better. You don't need to have everything figured out before reaching out.

From there, you can ask your primary care provider for a referral, check with your insurance company for in-network therapists, or search online directories like Psychology Today. Many therapists offer a brief free consultation call, which is a great opportunity to ask about their approach and see if you feel comfortable. When you attend your first session, know that it's okay to be unsure of what to say — the therapist is there to guide the conversation at a pace that works for you. Taking that first step takes courage, and it's perfectly normal to feel nervous.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response_text:
A good counselor typically needs strong communication skills, especially active listening—being able to truly hear and understand what someone is sharing without rushing to fix or judge. Empathy is essential, allowing the counselor to connect with a person's feelings and experiences in a genuine way. Patience and nonjudgmental acceptance help create a safe space where people feel comfortable opening up.

Beyond these interpersonal qualities, effective counselors also need good boundaries, self-awareness, and the ability to remain calm and grounded even when difficult emotions arise. They should understand when to gently guide a conversation and when to simply hold space for silence. Problem-solving and goal-setting skills matter too, as does ongoing self-reflection to recognize their own biases and limitations. If you're considering counseling—whether seeking one or becoming one—these are the qualities worth looking for or cultivating.

prompt: What are some difficulties that a counselor can encounter when dealing with a client?
response_text:
Counselors can encounter a range of challenges when working with clients. These may include resistance or reluctance to engage, difficulty building trust, and clients who struggle to articulate their feelings. Counselors also navigate complex situations like managing boundaries, addressing crises, and balancing empathy with professional objectivity. Additionally, clients may present with overlapping issues, such as co-occurring mental health conditions, that require careful assessment and collaboration with other professionals.

Counselors may also face emotional demands, as supporting others through distress can take a toll over time. Recognizing these challenges is an important part of the work, and many counselors use supervision, peer consultation, and self-care strategies to maintain their effectiveness and well-being. If you're exploring this topic for yourself or someone you know, reaching out to a qualified professional can provide more tailored guidance.
